title: Getting Schooled in School
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Underwood recounts his first years as a fourth grade teacher in 1986, moving from college teaching to a classroom he could not keep quiet, and the principal, workshops and colleagues who helped him learn. He describes a writing workshop where children chose projects, wrote for real audiences, and learned punctuation through peer teaching, and contrasts this with the disruption of standardized testing. From that experience he questions the factory metaphor for schools that scientific management bequeathed. Although he grants that routinized management has been necessary, the school he knew felt like a guild of devoted teachers rather than a plant. He ends by asking for a new shared metaphor that puts management in its place as an enabler.
points: A supportive principal who asked reflective questions and arranged mentoring turned a struggling novice into a capable teacher.
Real writing needs real audiences, which workshop structures, class magazines and parent readers can supply.
Assessment should speak to the future and strengthen the writer, and weeks of testing frenzy work against that.
The factory metaphor of scientific management is powerful but misdescribes the devotion teachers bring to children.
Management should be an enabler under a new organic metaphor rather than an objective monitor.
quotes: I could teach. I’d come to believe in myself. I just couldn’t keep a class full of youngsters quiet.
Her approach to post-observation conferences was consistent across all three of my precious fourth grade years. First question from her: How did you think it went?

Teaching them how to ask for meaningful feedback required them to identify for themselves problems and opportunities in their drafts, a strategy and habit of mind best taught through teacher modeling.
Assessment, to be worth its salt, must speak to the future, not the past. It must strengthen the writer with information, not reward or punish for past weakness.
The metaphor of the scientifically managed factory has been invoked by education reformers across generations to index a cruel and dehumanizing approach to schooling
At school I felt as though I were doing something bigger than me, I was a part of an ancient, voluntary guild doing significant and noble work. Teachers are remarkable people.
We need a new shared metaphor that puts management in its place as an enabler, not an objective monitor in a white coat or an FBI agent.
